   bones do to a weighted mesh as well as what a deform key does — unlike the
   `DEFORM` block, which compares a key against the same bones with the deform
   cleared.
2. **A region still in its bone's own frame.** Take the region's `slot`, look its
   `bone` up in `slots`, and for each frame carry its four corners into that bone's
   frame by the inverse of the bone's world transform:

   `det = a·d − b·c`, `dx = x − worldX`, `dy = y − worldY`,
   `lx = (d·dx − b·dy) / det`, `ly = (−c·dx + a·dy) / det`

   Against the same four carried from `setup`, the largest difference over frames is
   the region's motion *relative to its bone*: zero, to double rounding, for a region
   nothing but its bone moves. A face region measured against a head bone this way
   is the face with the head's own turn, translation and scale taken out.

**Measured on the example corpus** at 12 fps (these are one run's figures, not
thresholds): `spineboy-pro`'s eleven files total 5.1 MB, from 72 kB (`aim`, one
frame) to 1.46 MB (`death`, 60 frames), and `sack-pro`'s four 1.4 MB. The largest
stretch is `sack-pro` `fall-in`, `cape-back` triangle 15, ×6.744; the largest
still-in-frame residual over every region of `spineboy-pro` is 4.7e-12 world units
(`portal-streaks2`, whose bone scales; `sack-pro` has no region).
Topology and UVs sit in `rest` rather than on every frame because they do not
change: repeating them per frame would add 35 % to `spineboy-pro`'s files.

### 8.3 Which triangles fold — `render --folds`

A mesh can **fold** — a triangle turning over under a bend — on a build that passes
every assertion and every check. The art still draws, mirrored, over its neighbour,
and nothing in a report says so. `--folds` reads it off the frames `render` draws:

```bash
bun cli.ts render --candidate path/to/spine --folds [--animation …] [--skin …] [--fps 12]
# rigc render
#   ..    show             321 frame(s), 16.000s + contact.png + folds.json (2 of 11 mesh(es) fold) -> …/show@20fps
#   ..    folds    "show": mesh "hair_long" (slot "hair_long") folds on 88 frame(s) [33-54, 113-134, 194-215, 273-294] at 20 fps; worst frame 40 (t=2.0000s): 3 of 459 triangle(s) [137, 139, 140] in world box x [112.04, 133.28] y [323.01, 339.19] (21.22 × 16.16), setup-pose area 122.00 units² = 0.0686% of the mesh's; 3 triangle(s) fold on some frame [137, 139, 140]
```

**Where and how big.** The line says, for the worst frame, where the folded
triangles are — the **world box** of their vertices as posed at that frame, every
vertex of each and nothing else, printed rounded *outward* to hundredths so the
printed box still holds every one (the file states it exactly) — and how big they
are: their summed **setup-pose area**, each triangle's unsigned area in `rest`, in
world units², and that as a share of the mesh's own setup-pose area (every
triangle's, summed). "3 of 459 triangles" reads the same for three slivers at a
hair tip and three panels of a skirt; the share does not.

⭐ The box is the frame's and the area is the setup pose's, on purpose. The box is
where to look, so it is where the triangles are drawn. The area is how much of the
art is turned over, and a folded triangle's *posed* area cannot say that: it passes
through 0 at the frame the triangle turns, so one triangle reads a different size on
every frame it is folded — on the film above, `hair_long`'s three range from 0.09 to
24.2 units² posed across their 88 frames against 122.00 at the setup pose.

**What folded means.** A mesh triangle is folded at a frame when its orientation
there — the sign of its signed area in world space — is the opposite of its
orientation at the setup pose. The setup pose is `rest`'s (§8.2): the setup pose's
bones with no deform, so an attachment a slot only swaps to later is read too.
Regions are not read: a region is one quad and cannot fold. A mesh mirrored whole by
a negative scale reads every triangle as folded — that is what the definition says,
and the count tells the two apart.

**What is never counted.** A triangle already wrong at the setup pose is said once,
on a `setup` line the first time a set shows its mesh, and never counted:

- **degenerate** — its height over its longest edge is at most 2⁻³⁰ of the largest
  coordinate its attachment holds at that pose, in world space or in its UVs. That
  is eight million ulps above the rounding a chain of bone transforms leaves, and a
  hundred-thousandth of a pixel on a rig 10⁴ units across drawn at one pixel per
  unit — thinner than the posed numbers resolve, and thinner than anything drawn.
  A triangle degenerate *at a frame* is not counted at that frame either: the sign of
  a zero area is the rounding's;
- **inverted** — its texture is drawn mirrored against the rest of its mesh: the sign
  of world area × UV area is the opposite of the mesh's own sense, that product
  summed over its triangles, weighted by world area. Read through the UVs and not the
  index order, because the format fixes no winding — a mesh whose triangles are
  listed in mixed orders draws correctly, and a winding test would call half of it
  folded.

**The file.** `folds.json`, `rigc-folds/1`, beside each set's frames: `animation`,
`skin` (absent when none was set), `fps`, `reading` (these definitions, stated in
the file), and `meshes[]` — every mesh any frame of the set shows, in `rest`'s
order — each with `slot`, `attachment`, `triangleCount`, `setup` (`degenerate` and
`inverted`, triangle indices), `area` (the mesh's setup-pose area, world units²),
`frames[]` (only the frames with a folded triangle: `index`, `time`, `triangles`,
and that frame's `box` — `[minX, minY, maxX, maxY]`, world units, y up — `area` and
`share`, as above), `worst` (the frame with the most, the earliest on a tie, with the
same fields; `null` when it never folds) and `folded` (every triangle folded on some
frame). `area`, `box` and `share` arrived in 2.47 (issue #1386) as added fields:
every field 2.46 wrote means what it meant, so the tag is still `rigc-folds/1`.
A triangle is named by its index `i` in `rest`'s `triangles`: vertices
`triangles[3i]`, `triangles[3i+1]`, `triangles[3i+2]`. A mesh that never folds is in
the file and on no printed line.

**Nothing else moves.** The PNGs, `contact.png`, `frames.json` and, with
`--geometry` beside it, `geometry.json` are byte for byte what the render writes
without the flag. The reading is its own file rather than a field of `geometry.json`
because that file is the pose, read by consumers that have it on disk already; a
reading derived from it is computed from it — `foldsOf` over `geometry.json`'s
`rest` and `frames` is `folds.json` exactly (`FO04`). ⛔ **Not with
`--slot`/`--hide`**, for `--geometry`'s reason: the reading is of every mesh the pose
shows.

**A reading, not a gate.** Whether a fold is acceptable is yours: a tassel that swings
past 90° folds honestly, and no size is too small to print. To look at one, draw the
worst frame framed to it:
`inspect --show art,folds,mesh --animation <name> --at <worst time> --zoom folds`
fills the folded triangles at that pose, frames the picture to their box, and lists
them with the same box and area in its legend (§13).

### 8.4 The world the physics answers — `render --environment`

A physics constraint's `wind` and `gravity` are its **response** (§4.6); the world
it responds to — the two directions spine-core keeps on its `Skeleton` — belongs to
whoever plays the rig. A render has no player, so without this flag it draws every
frame in the runtime's initial world, wind `[1, 0]` and gravity `[0, 1]`.
`--environment` hands it one:

```bash
bun cli.ts render --candidate path/to/spine --environment gust.json [--animation …] [--geometry] [--poser core|spine]
```

```json
{
  "spec": "rigc-environment/1",
  "steps": [
    { "t": 0, "wind": [0, 0] },
    { "t": 1, "wind": [1.5, -0.4] },
    { "t": 2, "wind": [0, 0] }
  ]
}
```

**What a step means.** From its `t`, in seconds, until the next step, the world is
changed by the halves it states — `wind`, `gravity`, or both — and a half it leaves
out keeps the one standing, as a live track's `setEnvironment` keeps it. Both are
the runtime's own fields in the runtime's convention: x to the right, **y down** (a
positive y pulls toward the bottom of the frame, as gravity `[0, 1]` does). Before
the first step the world is the runtime's initial one, so a calm start is stated —
`"wind": [0, 0]` at `t` 0 — rather than assumed. Each set starts the schedule at its
own frame 0.

**When it lands.** A step's change is set before the step that poses the first
frame `i` whose time `i / fps` is at or after its `t`, so the physics integrates the
new world over that frame's whole interval and the frame before it is untouched.
Frame 0 is the reset pose; a step at `t` 0 is set before it. A `t` that is a frame's
own time — `k / fps` — lands on frame `k`.

**Both posers, one world.** The core sets each change on its physics before the
walk's step; spine-core's poser sets the same values on its `Skeleton` (`windX,
windY, gravityX, gravityY`) before the same update. The repository's selftest
renders three rigs — one answering wind and gravity on every branch of the physics
step, gallery/look with its whip answering wind, and a fixture answering gravity
alone — under a calm → gust → calm schedule through both, and holds every PNG,
`geometry.json` and `frames.json` equal (`RE01`); holds that the gust moves the rig
from its own frame and no earlier (`RE02`); and plants on the core the readings the
mapping rejects — the schedule ignored, its y read up, each change a frame late or
early — each red against spine-core (`RE03`).

**Whether the physics ran.** Every render — with this flag or without — says, under
each set's line, how many physics constraints the poser stepped on at least one of
its frames, and at what rate:

```text
  ..    idle             25 frame(s), 2.000s + contact.png -> render/idle
  ..    physics: 3 constraint(s) stepped at 12 fps
```

and `frames.json` carries the same two figures on that set, `"physics": { "stepped":
3, "fps": 12 }`. The rate is the set's own: one physics update a frame. The count is
read off the posed state, not off the declaration: a constraint counts when, after
a step that moved the skeleton's clock, its own clock reads the skeleton's — which
the physics update sets and every way of not running leaves behind. So a constraint
that is inactive on every frame, or at a mix of 0, is not counted, and the line names
it: `physics: 0 constraint(s) stepped at 12 fps — 1 of the 1 declared took none:
"iris_settle" (inactive, or a mix of 0, on every frame)`; a set of one pose — an
animation of no length, or the setup pose of a skeleton with none — takes no step
and says so. A rig that declares no physics constraint prints `physics: none in this
rig — it declares no physics constraint, so no frame steps one` once, before the
sets, and its `frames.json` carries no `physics` field, as every frame set written
before the field existed carries none. This is what tells a reading — a fold count
from `--folds`, say (§8.3) — taken with the physics from one taken without. Both
posers read the same constraints on every frame, and `cli.ts`, `cli.ts --poser
spine` and `cli_core.ts` write the same files (`PH01`, `PH02`); the step removed —
on the core, or spine-core's `PhysicsConstraint.update` made a no-op — reads 0
(`PH03`), and a constraint at mix 0 is named (`PH04`).

**The files.** `frames.json` and each `geometry.json` record the schedule as
`environment`, its steps as read, `t`, `wind`, `gravity` in that order. The
framing reads it too: a gust can carry a coat past the box a still rig fills, so
the box is the box of what the frames under the schedule draw — and the grid can
differ from the same render without the flag. Compare the two in world units, in
`geometry.json`. Without the flag nothing is set and every file is the bytes it
always was; the runtime's own world stated at `t` 0 draws the same pixels and
geometry as no flag at all (`RE04`). `check` poses its candidate in no world but
the runtime's, so a frame set drawn under a schedule is refused as a reference by
name rather than scored.

**Refused by name**, exit 2, nothing written — each is a render that would print a
plausible frame set showing nothing the schedule asked for (`RE05`):

- a path with nothing at it: `--environment <path>: nothing at <abs path>`;
- a file that is not one: `not JSON — …`, `the file holds <what>, not an object …`,
  `"spec" is <found>; render reads "rigc-environment/1"`, `the file names "<key>",
  which is not one of [spec, steps]`, `"steps" is <found>, not a non-empty array …`;
- an entry, by its index: `entry <i> of "steps" names "<key>", which is not one of
  [t, wind, gravity]`; `…'s "t" is <found>, not a finite time in seconds at or above
  0`; `…'s "t" is <found>, not after entry <i-1>'s <t> — steps are listed in
  ascending time, each holding until the next`; `…'s "wind" is <found>, not a pair
  of finite numbers [x, y] (x to the right, y down)` (`gravity` alike; a number the
  JSON reader makes infinite, `1e999`, is shown as `Infinity`); `… states neither
  "wind" nor "gravity", so it changes nothing`;
- a schedule this rig would not draw: a skeleton with no animation (its one frame
  is the setup pose, where no physics step runs) or no physics constraint; a half
  the schedule changes that no physics constraint answers — `entry <i> changes
  wind, and no physics constraint answers it — [<names>] each state wind 0 and no
  animation keys it`; two steps on one frame of the render's grid —
  `entries [<i>, <j>] (t …) land on one frame at <fps> fps — frame <k>, t=…s — so
  entry <i> would never be posed`; and a step after the last frame of every set
  drawn.

**What it is, and what it is not.** It is an inspection of the response the rig
states — what the Spine export carries, posed in a world you chose, on either
poser. It is not a scene: when a gust blows, how strong, and what else moves is the
consumer's to compose, and a schedule here is a probe of the object, not a
direction of it. Moving the rig is left out on purpose: `physicsTranslate` and
`physicsRotate` are a displacement since the last pose, which a step held over a
span would have to restate as a velocity — a second meaning the live track does
not have — and a render draws the rig where it stands, so the picture would show
a coat trailing a rig that never moves. The live track holds both to spine-core
(`CO56`), and a player forwards them as §4.6 says.

### 8.5 Where a cloth passes through a leg — `render --pass-through`

A skirt drawn over a thigh can swing its side straight through the thigh on a build
that passes every assertion and every check. A real skirt cannot do that while it is
in front of the leg: the leg is inside it and leaves through the hem. `--pass-through`
reads it off the frames `render` draws, for the pairs you name. On the selftest's
probe (`pass_through_probe`, `fixtures/public.ts`: a skirt whose hip swings 30° and
back over a leg it hangs in front of, and a second copy of the leg drawn over it):

```bash
bun cli.ts render --candidate path/to/spine --animation swing --pass-through skirt:leg,skirt:leg_front [--skin …] [--fps 12]
# rigc render
#   ..    swing            25 frame(s), 2.000s + contact.png + pass-through.json (1 of 2 pair(s) pass through) -> …/swing
#   ..    pass     "swing": cloth "skirt" over leg "leg" passes through on 21 of 25 frame(s) read [2-22] at 12 fps; deepest frame 11 (t=0.9167s): 23.00 units (23 step(s) of 1.0000) on its left side
#   ..    pass     "swing" frame 2 (t=0.1667s): cloth "skirt" over leg "leg" by 5.00 units (5 step(s) of 1.0000) on its left side, 44 row(s), in world box x [-27.48, -21.73] y [103.80, 147.08] (5.74 × 43.27)
#   …     one line for each of frames 3-22
#   ..    pass     "swing": cloth "skirt" over leg "leg_front": the cloth draws over the leg on 0 of 25 frame(s) both draw ("leg_front" draws over "skirt" wherever both draw) — nothing read
```

**Which frames are read.** A frame where both slots draw and the **cloth draws over
the leg**, in that frame's own draw order — a draw-order key that puts the leg in
front takes its frames out of the reading. The order in the flag is the
declaration: `skirt:leg` asks whether the skirt passes through the leg, and
`leg:skirt` is a different question, never the same one read both ways. A slot
paired with itself is read on no frame, and its line says why.

**What passing through means.** Four steps, every number in them derived:

1. **Rows, in the cloth's setup pose.** The cloth is drawn over its setup-pose
   geometry — `rest`'s vertices (§8.2), the setup pose's bones with no deform — at
   the frame's own UVs and tint, onto cells of **one texel of its drawing** as the
   setup pose lays it out. A cell is drawn when the renderer paints its centre at
   half opacity or more (128 of 255) — the line an antialiased edge sits on, rather
   than the faintest fringe the renderer would still paint. The rows are the setup
   pose's, not the world's, so a skirt the pose swings or bends still has its side
   where its side is: read in world rows, a waist the pose tilts becomes a "side"
   on the rows it spans, and a leg under it would read as passing through.
2. **The hem's corner.** On each side, the corner is the outermost drawn cell in the
   lower half of the drawn rows — the lowest on a tie. The rows from the corner up
   to the cloth's top are read; the rows below it are the hem's own curve, under
   which a leg is meant to show.
3. **The run.** On each read row, from the centre of the outermost drawn cell as the
   frame poses it, step outward — along the setup pose's outward direction, carried
   to the frame by the cloth triangle holding that centre — in **world units**, one
   texel of the coarser of the two drawings at a time, and count the steps whose
   point the leg draws at half opacity, up to the first it does not. That is how far
   the leg's outline passes the cloth's, in the units the picture shows.
4. **The line.** A frame passes through when some read row's run is **2 steps or
   more** — more than the one step an outline is resolved to.

⚠️ The run is in world steps, not in the cloth's setup-pose cells, because on a
cloth the pose squashes the two disagree: counted in setup cells, a run reads longer
than the picture holds, and the line printed a depth in units over a box narrower
than that depth. The rows are the setup pose's
because they say *which* part of the cloth is its side; the run is the world's
because it says *how far* the leg shows (`PX04`, and `PX12` plants the other).

**Blind spots, stated.** A cloth that widens all the way up to its waist has its
corner at mid-height, so the rows below are not read. A leg wholly beside the cloth,
entering above its top, meets no read row's side. And the rows are the setup pose's,
so a cloth authored lying on its side reads its side as a hem.

**The file.** `pass-through.json`, `rigc-pass-through/1`, beside each set's frames:
`animation`, `skin` (absent when none was set), `fps`, `reading` (these definitions,
stated in the file), and `pairs[]` in the flag's order, each with `cloth`, `leg`,
`drawn` (frames where both slots draw), `over` (of those, the frames the cloth draws
over the leg — the frames read), `frames[]` (only the frames that pass through:
`index`, `time`, `cells` — the longest run, in steps — `depth` — that in world
units — `cell` — the step — `side` — `left` or `right` of the cloth as it lies at its
setup pose — `attachment` — the cloth's at that frame — `rows` — read rows whose run
reaches the line — and `box` — `[minX, minY, maxX, maxY]`, world units, y up, over
both ends of every such run, the cloth's outline to the run's far end) and `deepest`
(the read frame with the longest run, the earliest on a tie, with `index`, `time`,
`cells`, `depth`, `cell` and `side`; `null` when no frame is read). A pair that passes
through on no frame is in the file, and its line says how many frames were read.

**Refused, nothing written:** a slot the skeleton does not have (with the slots it
does), an entry without exactly one `:`, an empty entry or name, a pair named twice,
a slot that draws on no frame of the sets drawn, a cloth or leg a clip cuts (its
drawing's outline is no longer its attachment's), and `--slot`/`--hide` beside the
flag, for `--folds`' reason.

**Nothing else moves.** The PNGs, `contact.png`, `frames.json` and `geometry.json`
are byte for byte what the render writes without the flag (`PX06`), and both posers
write the same file (`PX05`).

**A reading, not a gate.** It names frames and decides nothing: whether a frame that
passes through is a defect, and what to do about it — a leg stop, a wider hem, a
different swing — is yours. To look at one, draw it:
`inspect --show art --animation <name> --at <time> --zoom slot:<cloth>`.

### 8.6 One box for two renders — `render --viewport`, `render --viewport-from`

`render` fits its box to the rig it draws, so two builds of one rig — before and
after a change — usually land on two grids of different sizes, and their pixels
cannot be compared without a transform written by hand. Give the box instead:

```bash
bun cli.ts render --candidate before/ --out render-before
bun cli.ts render --candidate after/ --viewport-from render-before --out render-after
bun cli.ts render --candidate after/ --viewport -40,70,90,140 --max 256 --out render-box
```

- `--viewport-from <frames.json | dir>` reads an earlier render's `frames.json` (the
  file, or the directory `render --out` wrote it into) and draws on **its grid
  exactly**: the same world box, the same scale and the same pixel size, so a world
  point lands on the same pixel in both renders and the two frame sets overlay.
  `--max` is refused beside it, because the file already fixes the pixel size.
- `--viewport <x,y,w,h>` draws over a world box you state, y up, `x,y` its
  bottom-left corner — the numbers `frames.json`'s `viewport` records, and the
  spelling `check --viewport` and `inspect --viewport` take. Its pixel size follows
  from `--max` as a fitted box's does.

The render prints a `viewport given by …` line with the box and the box it would
have fitted, so you can see what the given one leaves out.

⚠️ **Nothing is cropped in silence.** Each frame is the box: what lies past it is
not drawn. A fitted box is measured over every pose the rig strikes at 60 fps and padded; a given one is not,
so every slot whose drawn geometry reaches past it — a piece's posed vertex outside
the box — is named, once per set: the frames, the farthest it reaches in world
units, and the sides (`left`, `right`, `bottom`, `top`, y up). `frames.json` records
the box was given and those slots under `pinned`: `{ "by": "--viewport" |
"--viewport-from", "outside": [{ "set", "slot", "frames" }] }` — written only when a
box was given, so a fitted render is the bytes it always was.

**Refused, nothing written:** the two flags together; `--max` beside
`--viewport-from`; a `--viewport` that is not four numbers or whose width or height
is not above 0; a `--viewport-from` path with no `frames.json`, a file whose `spec`
is not `rigc-frames/1`, and a `viewport` field that is not a finite number (`x`,
`y`), a number above 0 (`width`, `height`, `scale`) or a whole number of pixels above
0 (`pixelWidth`, `pixelHeight`) — each named with the value found. The framing still
runs under a given box, so a pose with nothing to draw, one that is not finite and
one with no extent are refused as they are without one.

### 8.7 How far a bone turns against another — `render --angle-range`

A physics value has no scale you can see from the spec: what `inertia` 0.5 does to
a link depends on its length, on how its parent moves and on every other value
together. The answer is a number the pose already holds — how far the link turned
against the bone it hangs from — and `--angle-range` reads it off the frames
`render` draws:

```bash
bun cli.ts render --candidate path/to/spine --angle-range tail:hip,sleeve:arm [--animation …] [--fps 12]
```

One line per pair per set, beside the set's line: the lowest and the highest angle
in degrees, the span, the frames read and the rate, and the frame each extreme was
first reached on. Nothing is written, and every file is the bytes the render writes
without the flag.

**What the angle is.** At each frame, the first bone's world direction less the
second's — each the direction its x axis points, degrees counter-clockwise, y up,
as the poser that drew the frame poses it (`rotationX`). The first frame's
difference is taken into (−180°, 180°], and each later frame's is moved by whole
turns to within half a turn of the frame before, so a link that sweeps 200° reads
200°, not −160°. ⚠️ It is the angle **drawn**, not the bone's local `rotation`: the
two agree for a child of the other bone when the parent carries no non-uniform scale
or shear.

**Where it is read.** On the frames' own grid — `--fps`, from t = 0 to each set's
last frame — so a peak between two frames is not read; raise `--fps` to read finer.
It reads bones, which `--slot`/`--hide` do not change, so it takes them.

**Refused, nothing written:** a bone the skeleton does not have (with the bones it
does), an entry without exactly one `:`, an empty entry or name, a bone against
itself (0° on every frame), a pair named twice, and a bone with no direction on a
frame — a world matrix of zero, which a bone the posed skin leaves unposed has, or
one scaled to nothing — named with the frame.

**A reading, not a gate.** Whether a range is too wide is yours; §4.6 says which
values move it.

### 8.8 Where two slots stop meeting — `render --seam`

A cut rig can tear in motion: two pieces painted to overlap at a joint pull apart
and the background shows between them, or one swings clear of the piece it was
tucked under and the overlap it carries shows where nothing was. Both pass every
assertion and every check, and either can be intended — so `--seam` names the
frames and decides nothing. On the selftest's probe (`pass_through_probe`,
`fixtures/public.ts`: a skirt whose hip swings 30° and back over a leg that hangs
inside it, and a second copy of the leg on the same bone):

```bash
bun cli.ts render --candidate path/to/spine --animation swing --seam skirt:leg,leg_front:leg [--skin …] [--fps 12]
# rigc render
#   ..    swing            25 frame(s), 2.000s + contact.png + seam.json (1 of 2 pair(s) open) -> …/swing
#   ..    seam     "swing": seam "skirt" | "leg" opens on 23 of 25 frame(s) read [1-23] at 12 fps, max 1606 px — gap on 13 frame(s) [6-18], worst frame 12 (t=1.0000s): 616 px (616.00 units² at 1.0000 units a px) in world box x [-7.00, 19.00] y [105.99, 196.00] (26.00 × 90.00); ghost on 23 frame(s) [1-23], worst frame 12 (t=1.0000s): 1606 px (1606.00 units² at 1.0000 units a px) in world box x [-27.00, 41.00] y [104.99, 198.00] (68.00 × 93.00)
#   ..    seam     "swing": seam "leg_front" | "leg" stays closed on all 25 frame(s) read at 12 fps — no gap, no ghost
```

The skirt swinging off the leg opens background between the leg's right edge and
the skirt's swung side (the gap, widest at the top of the swing), and uncovers the
top of the leg the skirt hid at rest (the ghost). The two copies of the leg move
on one bone and never open. A pair with nothing to read says so —
`seam "a" | "b": SKIP — the two drawings share no cell at the setup pose on any of
the N frame(s) both draw, so there is no band to read` — and a closed pair says
`stays closed on all N frame(s) read`; the two are never the same line.

**The frame of reference.** A seam is not read in the world: a limb that swings
moves both of its pieces from where they were at the setup pose, and that is
motion, not a tear. It is read **from each piece's own point of view**. A world
point of a frame is carried back into a piece's setup pose by the affine map of
that piece's triangle holding it as the frame poses it; outside the piece's mesh,
by the map of the triangle it is least outside of (the largest smallest
barycentric weight, the lowest index on a tie) — exact for a region and for any
mesh one bone moves, the nearest affine piece of a skinned one. Two pieces that
move together carry a point back to one place, so a pair moved whole reads nothing.

**Every number, and where it comes from.** Nothing here is a threshold the rig
did not declare; each figure is the posed vertices (`--geometry`'s), the rest
table's vertices, and the atlas alpha:

- **The cell** is one texel of the coarser of the two drawings at the setup pose,
  in world units — the step `--pass-through` steps by (§8.5) — on multiples of it
  from the world origin. `px` counts cells: on art drawn one texel to a unit, a
  cell is a world unit and a px is a pixel of the art.
- **Drawn** is the renderer painting a cell's centre at **128 of 255** or more —
  the half-opacity line `--pass-through` draws outlines at, the frame's tint
  included, the setup pose drawn at the same tint (so a slot faded out is not a
  tear: it is faded in both). This threshold defines the pair's band, gap and
  ghost; the composite coverage partition below asks a different question.
- **The band** is the cells both drawings draw at the setup pose — where the two
  were painted to overlap. It has **no width of its own**: it is the overlap the
  art states, dilated by nothing. A frame whose band is empty is not read; a pair
  whose band is empty on every frame both draw is a SKIP.
- **gap** — a cell inside the convex hull of the band's cell centres, carried to
  the frame by both pieces (the region the joint occupies now, as both place it),
  that neither piece draws at the frame, and that at least one piece, carrying it
  back, finds drawn by either drawing at the setup pose: the two no longer cover
  what they covered together. The hull is the joint's own extent, which is what
  keeps a piece's far end swinging away from reading as a tear; the rest test is
  what keeps a band that is concave at the setup pose from reading its own notch.
- **ghost** — a cell one piece draws at the frame and the other does not, which
  the drawing piece, carrying it back, lands in the band, and which the other,
  carrying it back, finds neither drawing at at the setup pose: the overlap swung
  clear of its partner.
- **ghostA**, **ghostB** — that same ghost partitioned by the piece drawing the
  cell: `a` only or `b` only, respectively, in the flag's named pair order. On
  each frame `ghost.px = ghostA.px + ghostB.px` (an absent hit contributes 0),
  and each owner's box lies inside the union's. Reversing the pair exchanges
  the complete owner readings and preserves `gap` and `ghost`.
- **gapOpen**, **gapCovered** — the same gap cells partitioned by the actual
  skeleton composite at their centres, on the same cell grid, over a transparent
  background: alpha **0** is open; alpha **>0** is covered. Every skeleton drawing
  enters, including the pair itself, with the frame's tint, UVs and clipping.
  Alpha **1..127 covers too**: this is not the pair's half-opacity outline test.
  The renderer's existing byte quantization remains in force: it emits rounded
  alpha only when the sampled, tinted value exceeds 0.5 on the 0..255 scale;
  a value that produces no rendered alpha byte is open. No display background
  enters. Source-over cannot erase positive alpha, so the renderer's positive
  emissions give exactly the nonzero alpha of its transparent composite.

On every frame `gap.px = gapOpen.px + gapCovered.px` (missing hit means 0).
Each partition's box lies in the union's. A gap in the pair can be covered by a
third drawing and need not be a visible opening. Reversing the pair preserves
both gap coverage readings.

Draw order does not enter: a cell is covered or bare whichever piece is in front.
An owner says which piece drew a ghost cell; it does not say which piece is over
or under the other, or whether that exposure should fail a consumer's policy.

**Outside the overlap hull is outside the gap reading.** Both `gap` and its
`gapOpen` partition are judged only inside the carried setup-overlap hull. Art
that reaches beyond a joint disc, such as a drape over an elbow, can break
outside that hull without a gap being reported. A gap of 0 is never a statement
that the seam is closed outside the hull; inspect `ghost` and the actual frames
too. Ghost independently names one-sided exposure of the carried setup overlap,
not every visible break in the silhouette.

In the public [draped-sleeve fixture](https://github.com/rig-c/parts/blob/0628d7bc311a2b548edf7a11e8407546357d4b4d/fixtures/hybrid_limb.ts),
measured on core `f273358` at both −30° and +30°, the hard cut reads `gap = 0`,
`gapOpen = 0`, `ghost = 8` cells; the hybrid's two interfaces read 0 in all three
classes. The [cell overlay](https://github.com/rig-c/core/blob/570a2954747780a2169fa6036eebe53f3ea66f2a/bench/studies/2026-10-25-seam-reach/evidence/cut-endpoint-cell-overlay.png)
shows the notch and flap excluded outside the hull, while ghost names different
cells on the joint rim. The [measurement receipt](https://github.com/rig-c/core/blob/570a2954747780a2169fa6036eebe53f3ea66f2a/bench/studies/2026-10-25-seam-reach/evidence/receipt.json)
pins the inputs, commands and frame digest; these are seam cells, not display
pixels. See [#1575](https://github.com/rig-c/core/issues/1575) for the reading.

**Its reach, stated.** A piece folded right back over its partner carries the band
across the region it vacated, so a hull that wide reads the vacated cells its
partner's view still finds drawn. And no size is too small to print: on
`gallery/walk`, built as its README says, `--seam thigh_f:shin_f,arm_f:hand_f`
reads gaps of 1–2 px on 5 of the 12 frames at the knee and of 1 px on 2 at the
wrist — the wrist's, drawn at 20 pixels a unit, is the V where the two outlines
meet at an angle, one cell deep. Whether that is a tear is yours.

**The file.** `seam.json`, `rigc-seam/1`, beside each set's frames — the contract
a consumer reads it by. Every unit is in this table; the file's own `reading`
block carries the definitions above in words.

| Field | Type | Unit | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `spec` | string | — | `"rigc-seam/1"` |
| `animation` | string or `null` | — | the set's animation; `null` for a skeleton with none (its one frame is the setup pose) |
| `skin` | string | — | the skin asked for; **absent** when none was |
| `fps` | number | frames per second | the rate the set was sampled at |
| `reading` | object | — | `read`, `cell`, `drawn`, `band`, `carried`, `gap`, `ghost`, `box`, `status`, `ghostA`, `ghostB`, `gapOpen`, `gapCovered`: the definitions, in words |
| `pairs[]` | array | — | one per pair, in the flag's order |
| `pairs[].a`, `pairs[].b` | string | — | the two slots, as the flag names them |
| `pairs[].drawn` | integer | frames | frames on which both slots draw |
| `pairs[].banded` | integer | frames | of those, frames whose two drawings share a cell at the setup pose — the frames read |
| `pairs[].status` | `"read"` or `"skip"` | — | `skip` when `banded` is 0: nothing measured, which is **not** a seam that held |
| `pairs[].opens` | integer[] | frame indices | every frame with a gap or a ghost, ascending |
| `pairs[].maxPx` | integer | px (cells) | the most cells of either kind on any frame; 0 when none opens |
| `pairs[].gap`, `pairs[].ghost` | object | — | one per kind, each `{ frames, spans, worst }` |
| `pairs[].ghostA`, `pairs[].ghostB` | object | — | the same `{ frames, spans, worst }` shape for ghost cells drawn by `a` only and `b` only; an empty owner has `frames: []`, `spans: []`, `worst: null` |
| `pairs[].gapOpen`, `pairs[].gapCovered` | object | — | the same `{ frames, spans, worst }` shape for gap cells with zero or positive rendered skeleton-composite alpha, respectively; an empty kind has `frames: []`, `spans: []`, `worst: null` |
| `<kind>.frames[]` | hit[] | — | only the frames with a cell of that kind, in frame order |
| `<kind>.spans[]` | array | — | `<kind>.frames` as runs of consecutive indices: `{ frames: [first, last], times: [first, last], maxPx }` — frame indices, seconds, px |
| `<kind>.worst` | hit or `null` | — | the frame with the most cells, the earliest on a tie; `null` when none |
| hit `index` | integer | frame index | the frame — `f<index>.png`, zero-padded |
| hit `time` | number | seconds | the frame's time |
| hit `px` | integer | px (cells) | cells of that kind on the frame |
| hit `cell` | number | world units | a cell's side |
| hit `area` | number | world units² | `px × cell²` |
| hit `box` | `[minX, minY, maxX, maxY]` | world units, y up | the counted cells' whole squares, in Spine world |

A downstream warning is a projection of this file and needs nothing re-measured:
one span of one kind is `{ pair: "<a>|<b>", frames: span.frames, times:
span.times, maxPx: span.maxPx, kind }`, and one pair over one animation is
`opens.length` frame(s) `[opens]`, max `maxPx` px — with `status: "skip"` the case
to say SKIP for.

The owner keys and their two legend entries are additive in `rigc-seam/1`.
Removing just those four keys leaves the previous file's bytes after the same
two-space JSON serialization and newline. The union, its spans and worst, and
the printed summary retain their existing meanings; an owner may have different
spans or a different worst frame from the union.
Likewise `gapOpen`, `gapCovered` and their two legend entries are additive:
removing only those entries leaves the previous file's bytes after the same
serialization, including `gap`, `ghostA` and `ghostB`. The coverage partition may
have different spans and worst frames from the union; it changes no seam policy.

**Refused, nothing written:** a slot the skeleton does not have (with the slots it
does), an entry without exactly one `:`, an empty entry or name, a slot paired with
itself (a seam is between two drawings), a pair named twice in either order (the
reading is symmetric, so `b:a` is `a:b` again), a slot that draws on no frame of
the sets drawn, a slot a clip cuts (its drawing is no longer its attachment's, so
it cannot be carried back), and `--slot`/`--hide` beside the flag, for
`--pass-through`'s reason.

**Nothing else moves.** The PNGs, `contact.png`, `frames.json` and `geometry.json`
are byte for byte what the render writes without the flag, both posers write the
same file, and two runs write the same bytes (the selftest's `seam` suite).

**A reading, not a gate.** It never changes the exit status, whatever it finds. To
look at a frame it names, draw that set over the box it printed:
`render --animation <name> --viewport <x,y,w,h> --max 400`.

### 8.9 Which slot covers which — `render --overlaps`

An arm the draw order puts behind the torso simply vanishes from the frames, on a
build that passes every assertion and every check, and nothing in the frames names
it. `--overlaps` reads it off the frames `render` draws: **who covers whom, on which
frames, by how many pixels**. On the selftest's probe (`overlap_probe`,
`fixtures/public.ts`: an opaque stage, a still body, and an arm drawn after the body
slid along x across it and out the other side):

```bash
bun cli.ts render --candidate path/to/spine --animation cross --overlaps --max 160 [--skin …] [--fps 12]
# rigc render
#   ..    cross            25 frame(s), 2.000s + contact.png + overlaps.json (1 moving pair(s), 11 outline plate(s)) -> …/cross
#   ..    overlap  "cross": 2 pair(s) cover on every frame by the same pixels, or with the slot in front drawn wholly on the one behind — layering the motion does not move; overlaps.json lists them
#   ..    overlap  "cross": OVERLAP "body" under "arm": frames 7–17 (11 of 25), covered up to 135 px at frame 11
```

⭐ **The render reports what was drawn; who should be in front is the author's, and
the draw-order key in the motion spec is the remedy** (§4.7, `drawOrder`). The same
slide with a key that puts the arm before the body reads `OVERLAP "arm" under
"body"` on the same frames and pixels (`OX02`). On `gallery/walk` at `--fps 20 --max
288` the back arm reads `OVERLAP "arm_b" under "torso": frames 0–18 (19 of 19),
covered up to 643 px at frame 15`; with `arm_b` moved after `torso` in the rig's
slots, that line is gone and `OVERLAP "torso" under "arm_b"` reads the same 643 px at
frame 15.

**Which frames are read.** Every frame of every set drawn, in **that frame's own
draw order** — the order its pieces are drawn in, so a draw-order key is honoured.

**What covering means.** Every piece is rasterised in draw order on the render's own
viewport, so a pixel here is a pixel of `f<NNNN>.png`. A pixel is drawn by a slot
when the renderer paints it at half opacity or more (128 of 255) — the line every
other reading draws outlines at. Each pixel keeps the slots that have drawn it so
far; a slot drawing a pixel earlier slots already drew **covers** each of them there,
one pixel to each (earlier, later) pair. `under` is the earlier-drawn slot, `over`
the later-drawn one. Pairs are by slot name, so `a` under `b` and `b` under `a` —
one draw-order key apart — are two pairs.

**Layering the motion does not move.** A pair that covers on **every** frame, and on
each either by the **same** pixel count or with the slot in front drawn **wholly on**
the one behind (every pixel `over` draws is one `under` drew first), is static
layering: a backdrop under a part that never leaves it, a face drawn over the head
that carries it. It is counted on one line and listed in the file, never printed
pair by pair. ⚠️ The pixel count alone was measured not to be enough: on
`gallery/walk`, a part turning over the backdrop changes its pixel count from frame to
frame by rasterisation alone, so none of its 35 pairs read as static and 14 backdrop lines (and the eyes over the head) buried the ones that mattered.
Every other pair that covers anything prints one `OVERLAP` line; a pair that never
covers prints nothing.

**Blind spots, stated.** A fringe painted under half opacity covers nothing here
although it tints the frame. A slot in front lying wholly on the one behind on every
frame reads as layering however it moves across it — an arm swung over the torso
without ever leaving it. A slot drawing more than one piece is one slot. And the
counts are pixels at the render's `--max`: quote the size beside a figure.

**The file.** `overlaps.json`, `rigc-overlaps/1`, beside each set's frames:
`animation`, `skin` (absent when none was set), `fps`, `reading` (`drawnAlpha` 128,
`unit` `"frame pixels"`, and `rule`, the definition above), `frames[]` — every
frame, with `index`, `time` and `pairs[]` (`under`, `over`, `px`, and `box`
`[x0, y0, x1, y1]`: frame pixels, x right, y down, both ends inclusive) — and
`pairs[]`, one per pair that covers on any frame: `under`, `over`, `frames` (how
many it covers on), `of` (the set's frames), `runs` (`[[first, last], …]`,
inclusive), `most` (`{ index, px }`, the earliest on a tie), `inside` (the slot in
front wholly on the one behind on every frame it covers on) and `varies` (`false`
for static layering). Both lists are ordered by `under`, then `over`, by code unit.

**The outline plate.** `overlaps-f<NNNN>.png`, numbered as the frames are, for each
frame where a moving pair covers: a white plate of the frame's size; every slot in a
moving pair drawn as its **contour** — a drawn pixel with an undrawn neighbour left,
right, above or below — in its own colour, in draw order; a contour pixel some slot
drawn later also drew is **dashed** (drawn where `(x + y) % 4 < 2`); and the slot's
name, spelled as the lines spell it (`arm_b`, not `ARM_B`). Names are placed in draw
order and no two touch: each takes the first free box, trying for every contour pixel
in raster order (the first is the topmost, the leftmost on a tie) the box above it,
below it, to its left and to its right; when none is free, the free spot nearest the
topmost pixel, joined to it by a one-pixel leader line; every box clamped inside the
plate. A plate with no free spot left prints the name at its first box anyway — the
one case two names can meet. A slot keeps one colour across a set's plates (a fixed table of eight,
by the slot's place among the set's moving slots in code-unit order); the colour
means only "another slot" — the name says which.

**`frames.json`.** Each set gains `overlaps`: `file`, `pairs` (how many cover on any
frame), `static` (how many of those are layering), `plates`, and `moving[]` — each
moving pair's `under`, `over`, `frames` and `most` — so a reader that cannot open a
plate has the figures.

**Refused, nothing written:** `--slot`/`--hide` beside the flag. A slot left out
covers nothing, so the pairs it is in would vanish and the reading would describe a
picture of part of the rig — run `render --overlaps` on the whole rig and the subset
without it; both land on one grid.

**Nothing else moves.** The PNGs, `contact.png` and every other file are byte for
byte what the render writes without the flag, and `frames.json` differs only by
each set's `overlaps` record (`OX05`); two runs and both posers write the same file
and plates (`OX04`).

**A reading, not a gate.** It never changes the exit status. Whether a covered arm
is a defect is yours; when it is, the remedy is a `drawOrder` key in the motion
spec (or the slot's place in the rig's `slots`), and the next render says whether
the line moved.

### 8.10 Sprite sheets from a render — `render --sheet`

```bash
bun cli.ts render --candidate path/to/build --sheet [--sheet-format json-hash] [--page-edges pot|free] [--animation idle] [--fps 12] [--max 256]
```

Packs each rendered animation set into a deterministic, transparent sprite sheet
beside the diagnostic frames, with a TexturePacker JSON Hash descriptor per page
and a rigc manifest stating the source identities, provenance, and coordinate
contract.

**What it writes per set (`<out>/<set>/`):**

- `sheet.png` and `sheet.json` (plus `sheet2.png`, `sheet2.json`, … when a set
  spills across `2048 × 2048` pages) — RGBA PNG pages rendered over transparent
  `[0, 0, 0, 0]` (`alphaMode: "straight"`), packed through `packAtlas` with a
  fixed `2048` page ceiling and `2`-px clamped edge extrusion around every cell.
  `--page-edges pot` (the default) rounds each page edge up to a power of two;
  `--page-edges free` sizes each page tightly to the packed cells plus their
  `2`-px border.
- `sheet-manifest.json` (`spec: "rigc-sheet/1"`) — the set's machine-readable
  provenance and coordinate contract: `format` (`"json-hash"`), `namespace`,
  `source` (`{ skeleton: { file, sha256 }, model: { file, sha256 } | null }`,
  recording the relative filenames and SHA-256 digests of the `skeleton.json`
  and `skeleton.model.json` the sheet was rendered from, with no paths),
  `animation` (`null` on a setup-pose set), optional `skin` / `slots` / `hidden` /
  `environment` / `pinned`, `fps`, `duration`, `sampled`, `endpointPolicy`
  (`"inclusive-grid"`), `alphaMode` (`"straight"`), `filterPolicy`
  (`{ recommended: "linear", paddingPx: 2, extrusion: "clamp-edge" }`),
  `pageEdges`, `pageSize` (`2048`), `padding` (`2`), `sourceSize` (`{ w, h }`),
  `viewport`, `pivot` (`{ world: [0, 0], canvasPx: { x, y }, anchor: { x, y } }`),
  `pages[]` (`{ index, image, table, width, height, occupancy, frames }`),
  and `frames[]` in chronological `0 .. N - 1` order (`{ index, key, time, page, image, table, empty, frame, spriteSourceSize, sourceSize, anchor }`).
- `frames.json` gains `sheet` on each set entry (`manifest`, `format`,
  `pageEdges`, `pages`, `frames`, `emptyFrames`).

**What does not move.** The diagnostic `f####.png` frames and `contact.png` stay
drawn over `BACKGROUND` (`[232, 232, 232, 255]`) and are byte for byte what `render`
writes without `--sheet`; stripping `sheet` from each set in `frames.json`
leaves the plain render's `frames.json` to the byte (`SH02`). Two runs and both
posers (`--poser core` and `--poser spine`) write the same `sheet*.png`,
`sheet*.json`, and `sheet-manifest.json` byte for byte (`SH03`), with no
timestamps, host strings, or absolute paths.

**Trimming, empty frames, and `alpha > 0`.** Every frame is rendered at the
set's full canvas (`sourceSize: { w: viewport.width, h: viewport.height }`) over
straight-alpha `[0, 0, 0, 0]` and trimmed to the minimal bounding box of pixels
with `alpha > 0` (`alpha >= 1`), preserving `alpha === 1` feather edges (`SH13`)
and un-premultiplied RGB channels (`SH14`). When every pixel on a frame has
`alpha === 0` (for instance, when `--hide` or `--slot` hides every visible slot
on that step), the frame is emitted as a `1 × 1` transparent `[0, 0, 0, 0]`
sentinel cell (`empty: true`, `trimmed: true`,
`spriteSourceSize: { x: 0, y: 0, w: 1, h: 1 }`, `sourceSize` preserved) so the
animation's frame count and timing stay intact and reconstructing the frame
yields an all-zero full canvas (`SH12`).

**Shared world `(0, 0)` anchor and multi-page layout.**

- Each entry in `frames` carries `"anchor": { "x": ax, "y": ay }`, where
  `canvasPx = projector(viewport)(0, 0)` projects Spine world `(0, 0)` into
  untrimmed canvas pixel coordinates and `ax = canvasPx.x / viewport.width`,
  `ay = canvasPx.y / viewport.height`. When a pinned `--viewport` excludes world
  `(0, 0)`, `ax` and `ay` are preserved un-clamped outside `[0, 1]` so placing a
  sprite at `(worldOriginX, worldOriginY)` still lands every pixel at its exact
  world coordinate (`SH15`).
- Each `sheet*.json` carries `frames`, `animations`, and `meta` (`app: "rig-c"`,
  `format: "RGBA8888"`, `image`, `size: { w, h }` as a single object and never an
  array, and `scale: "1"`). When a set spills across multiple pages, `packAtlas`
  assigns trimmed cells to pages by descending area rather than by frame time:
  each page's `frames` and `animations[<namespace>]` list only the frames that
  landed on that page (ordered chronologically within that page), `meta.related_multi_packs`
  names the sibling descriptor files (`SH16`), and the full set's playback order
  across all pages comes from `sheet-manifest.json`'s `frames[]` (`0 .. N - 1`).

**Collision-free frame keys and sampling policy.** Frame keys are
`<rig>/<set>[/<variants>]/f<NNNN>` (for example, `squash/bounce/f0000` at the
default `12` fps or `squash/bounce@24fps/skin=alt/f0000` at `24` fps under
`--skin alt`), where `<rig>` is derived from `rig.archetype` in
`skeleton.model.json` (the rig spec's `name`, never the build output folder) and
`<set>` is `frameSetDir(animation, fps)`, so rendering one animation at different
rates or copying a build into differently named folders never collides or moves
a byte (`SH04`, `SH17`, `SH19`, `SH20`). Sampling follows `render`'s closed grid
(`[0, duration]` at `Math.round(duration * fps) + 1` frames, recorded as
`endpointPolicy: "inclusive-grid"`): whether a looping playback drops the
closing endpoint frame or plays the full grid is a scene playback decision left
to the consumer.

**Self-check, external reader verification, and refusals.** Before any file is
written, `verifySheetPack`
reconstructs every frame from the packed `sheet*.png` pages and `sheet*.json`
descriptors onto a blank `sourceSize.w × sourceSize.h` canvas and checks that
every reconstructed canvas is byte-identical (`0` differing RGBA bytes) to the
untrimmed transparent render (`SH05`), that every cell's `2`-px border is
clamped edge extrusion (`SH06`), that no two padded cells overlap (`SH07`–`SH11`),
and that `source` records relative filenames and valid 64-hex SHA-256 digests (`SH21`).
On a source checkout, `bun tools/sheet_readers.ts --sheet <dir>` loads a packed
set (single-page or multi-page via `meta.related_multi_packs`) in headless
Playwright Chromium through the pinned `pixi.js@8.22.0` (`PIXI.Assets.load` /
`PIXI.Spritesheet`) and `phaser@3.90.0` (`Phaser.Textures.Parsers.JSONHash` /
`addAtlasJSONHash`) loaders and checks cut rectangles, `sourceSize` and
`spriteSourceSize`, `defaultAnchor` / `customPivot` alignment at
`pivot.canvasPx` (`0` px drift; in Phaser 3.86+, set `roundPixels: false` on the
game or camera when `pivot.canvasPx` is sub-pixel so `CanvasRenderer` does not
round the sprite translation before adding `-displayOrigin + frame.{x,y}`),
chronological playback order, multipage membership, and straight-alpha rendering
over light (`[232, 232, 232, 255]`) and dark (`[28, 28, 32, 255]`) backgrounds;
`SH22`–`SH25` hold its host-side refusals.
`--sheet-format` with an unknown value or without `--sheet`, `--page-edges` on
`render` without `--sheet` or with an unknown value, and any frame whose trimmed
bounds plus its `2`-px border on each side exceed `2048` (`w + 4 > 2048` or
`h + 4 > 2048`) are refused by name, exit 2, with nothing written (`SH17`).

---

## 9. Checking against the frames — `rigc check`

```bash
bun cli.ts check --candidate path/to/spine --frames path/to/reference/frames
```

`--frames` takes either a **skeleton root** (the directory holding `frames.json`,
which checks every animation of that shot, framed per set — see the scope note
below) or **one animation directory** inside it. Everything else is optional:
`--atlas` when the candidate's atlas is not beside its skeleton, `--as <name>` when
your animation is called something the frame directory is not, `--framing shared`
to fit one framing across every set instead of one each,
`--texture-from <atlas>` to attribute how much of the MAE is texture resampling
rather than the rig (**§9.2**'s atlas floor — and note that it is *not* `--atlas`,
which re-seats your geometry on that atlas's packing), `--skin <name>` to pose
your candidate under one of its skins (below), `--all-frames` to list
every frame instead of the worst by MAE, `--json <out>` for the whole per-frame,
per-slot report, `--out <dir>` for the picture each listed frame's figures came from
(**§9.2.1**).

🚨 **What `check` certifies is the DEFAULT skin, unless you pass `--skin`.** With no `--skin` no skin is set at all, which is `spine-core`'s own
initial state: every slot resolves through `SkeletonData.defaultSkin` alone, and a
slot whose art lives only in a named skin draws **nothing** — on both sides, since
the reference frames came out of the same renderer. A multi-skin rig checked that
way compares blank against blank and reports `MAE mean 0.00`, which reads like the
best possible answer and is a measurement of no art at all. On a single-skin rig
this is the whole rig and there is nothing to pass.

So a multi-skin rig is checked **once per skin**, and both sides are rendered
under the same one:

```bash
bun cli.ts render --candidate path/to/spine --skin patch --out frames/patch
bun cli.ts check  --candidate path/to/spine --frames frames/patch --skin patch
```

Three things keep that honest, and none of them is a convention you have to
remember:

- `render --skin` writes the name into `frames.json`, so a frame set says which
  picture of the rig it is. A set rendered with **no** `--skin` records nothing,
  because "no skin was set" and "this file predates the field" are the same bytes
  on disk and neither is a claim.
- `check` reads that back. A candidate posed under a **different** skin from the
  one the frames record — or under none, where the frames name one — is
  **refused by name** rather than scored, because the number would be about the
  difference between two skins. Frames that record nothing cannot be checked, and
  the report says so in a `⚠️` note instead of implying agreement.
- The report header names the skin on both sides on every run, `--skin` or not:
  `skin  candidate patch   frames patch`, or `candidate no skin set (the default
  skin alone)`. `check.json` carries the same two under `skin` and
  `referenceSkin`.

🔎 **The report also names the poser that drew the candidate**, on a `poser` line
under `skin`, in the words `render` prints (issue #968):
`poser      rigc core — …/skeleton.model.json` for a rigc build the core poses, and
`poser      spine-core — <why>` otherwise, `<why>` in the words the `--poser` row of
the flag table near the top lists — a Spine export (`no skeleton.model.json
beside …`), a `skeleton.json` edited after the build (both digests named), a
refusal of the core's, or `--poser spine`, among them. `check.json` carries it as
`"poser": { "name": "core" | "spine", "note": "<the line>" }`, and `--out`'s
`frames.json` under `comparison.poser`. One choice per run: every set, the setup
pose and the non-finite sentence are posed through the same poser, and a core
refusal partway re-poses all of it on spine-core. `--poser core|spine` forces the
choice with `render`'s semantics (`core` on an input that cannot carry it exits 2,
nothing written). The two posers are measured to write the same report, byte for
byte but the poser line, on every tree row.

A skin name the candidate does not declare is refused with the ones it does —
`the candidate declares no skin "path"; it declares [default, patch, torn]`.

🚫 **A frame set of PART of a rig is not a reference.** `render --slot`/`--hide`
(§0) records the subset in `frames.json`, and `check` refuses any set that carries
`slots` or `hidden`, before posing anything:

```
rigc check error: --frames frames/ records a slot subset (hidden: head) in frames.json; a partial render is not a reference set — render the reference without --slot/--hide
```

It is the skin clause one step stronger: two skins are two pictures of one rig,
while a reference with a part left out is not a picture of the whole rig at all,
and scoring a whole candidate against it would print a real figure about art the
reference never drew. There is no flag that makes it comparable. A set with
neither key — every set rendered without the flags, and every set written before
they existed — is compared exactly as before.

📌 **Deform measurement needs no such flag, because the timeline carries the
name.** `A39` and the `DEFORM` block pose each key with the skin that key is keyed
on — a deform timeline's address is a `skin / slot / attachment` triple — so a
mesh in a named skin is measured in that skin without anything being passed on the
command line (§4.11.5). The difference is where the name comes from,
not which command cares: `check` compares two picture sets and neither of them
records a skin unless you say so, while a deform key knows its own.

⭐ **A frame set may ship a contact sheet instead of every frame, and the sheet is
compared too.** A long shot does not commit 311 near-duplicate PNGs: rung 2's sets
ship `f0000.png` and `f0310.png` plus a `contact.png` holding all 311 sampled
frames, and spineboy's `@30fps` sets do the same. The frame table still says
`frames 2 on disk, candidate samples 311, 2 compared` — those are the files — and a
**`sheet` line under it** carries the other 309: your candidate sampled at the set's
own rate, rendered into the same box the frames above were at the sheet's own scale,
and compared tile by tile.

⚠️ **Read it as a series, not as one number** — §9.2. And note what it does not
carry: MAE only. The `Δpx` / `ref Δ` thresholds are calibrated at frame scale and a
tile has a fraction of a frame's pixels, so the per-frame change measure stays on
the committed stills, where it reports `no two compared frames are adjacent` and
means it.

⭐ **Do not treat such a set's two stills as bookends. They are full-resolution frames
at their own rate, and one of them is routinely a pose no other set on disk carries.**
The temptation is to read a strided set as *a sheet, plus two files that fix the
framing* — the sheet is where the shot is, so the stills look like plumbing. But the
last still is the animation's **own last sample at that rate**, and a finer rate lands
on a different instant: a shot whose length is not a multiple of the coarse interval
ends *between* two coarse samples, so the coarse set's last frame is not the end of the
shot and the finer set's is. If the shot is still moving there — and an end pose usually
is the part that moves most — that pose exists in exactly one file, at full resolution,
and it is worth fitting like any other frame.

⇒ **Two consequences for a run.** ① **Fit every committed still**, at every rate, and
do not let a "sheets are for timing" habit skip them; a pose you never fitted is a pose
you guessed, and a hold written across the gap because nothing on disk contradicted it
is a **fabrication** rather than a simplification. ② This is the same fact a brief
states from the timing side when it warns you against declaring the coarse set's
rounded length: the rounding and the missing pose are one arithmetic, seen twice. If
your shot's length is not a whole number of coarse intervals, expect **both** — a
duration the coarse sidecar understates, and a terminal pose only the finer set shows
you.

`--fps <n>` exists for frame sets that have no `frames.json` beside them: it gives
the rate those frames were
sampled at, and without it the 12 fps protocol rate is assumed and the report says
so rather than letting the assumption look like a measurement. Passing `--fps` with
a value the sidecar contradicts is an error, not an override.

A set with no sidecar is one of two things, and the `⚠️ no frames.json` note says
which advice goes with which: **a rigc render older than the sidecar** is fixed by
rendering it again with `rigc render`, and **a foreign source** — a Live2D, Unity or
video player, whose frames predate nothing — needs the three things the sidecar
would have said, supplied by whoever made them: an opaque background of the colour
the note names, `--fps` at the rate it was rendered, and a directory named after
the candidate animation it shows or `--as <that animation>`. Two of those are
refused by name when they are wrong, because a figure would come out of either:

```
rigc check error: --frames frames/turn has no frames.json, and 24 of its 24 compared reference frame(s) are not opaque (f0000.png, f0001.png, f0002.png, and 21 more): f0000.png has alpha 0 at (0, 0), where every pixel must be 255. Without a sidecar the frames are read against the background colour 232, 232, 232, 255 with alpha unread, so a pixel that is not opaque counts by its colour bytes alone: a transparent background counts as drawn and puts the figure over the whole frame, a number about the transparent area and not the rig, which --viewport does not change. Render the frames onto an opaque background of 232, 232, 232, 255.
rigc check error: no reference frame could be compared, so there is nothing to frame against: the frames were matched to a candidate animation by name, and the candidate has no animation called "idle" (the directory's own name) — it declares [sweep, tilt, turn]. Pass --as <name> with the one these frames show, or name the directory after it
```

The test is every pixel's alpha, not the border's: a pixel that is not opaque is
not yet a colour — what it shows depends on what it is composited over — so one
pixel of alpha 254 in one frame is refused too, naming that frame and that pixel.
The first is a refusal rather than a note because pinning does not rescue it:
`--viewport` set to the box the frames were drawn in reads MAE **0.00** on the
opaque set and **32.90** on the same set made transparent, on every one of its 24
frames — the transparent area times its distance from the background colour, which
is a figure about the background and not about the rig. `--as` takes **one**
candidate animation name; the `<candidate>=<reference>` pair is `diff`'s spelling,
and `check` refuses it as a name the candidate does not declare.

`--viewport <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>` pins your candidate's world box instead of
fitting it. Two uses:

- the derivation cannot work — a candidate deliberately missing a part has a
  different content box by construction, and pinning lets the rest of the shot
  still be measured;
- you want the framing **held still** between builds. The framing line is still
  measured and printed when the box is pinned, so a pinned run separates "my keys
  moved" from "my framing moved" without either hiding the other. On a shot whose
  MAE moves by more than a point for a fraction of a pixel, that separation is
  worth more than the absolute number.

A third use — *"you already know your candidate's world coordinates match the
reference's own, declared in `frames.json`"* — is one **`check` covers for you.** Before
fitting anything it renders your candidate
into the box `frames.json` records and measures where your pixels land. If they
land on the reference's to within a pixel, that box is yours too, and it is used:
it is not an *estimate* of where the frames were drawn, it is where they were
drawn, and the framing line says `frames.json's own box — the candidate measured
into it`. If they do not, the box is refused and your candidate is framed by its
own pixels — which is the ordinary case, because the reference's
origin is in a file you are not allowed to open.

That is worth a paragraph rather than a line because of what it costs when it is
missing. The fit is registered on **extent**, and extent is not alignment (see the
⚠️ in §9.2), so on a shot whose silhouette differs anywhere it lands a fraction of
a percent away from the framing the frames were drawn at — and a fraction of a
percent of scale is worth several MAE. Measured on rung 6: **8.73 fitted against
3.50 in the frames' own box**, with every content box, residual and rms already
under the method's noise. Rung 5 measured the same gap, 12.49 against 4.35. Neither
author could tell that from a wrong animation without running the pin by hand.

Pinning to paper over a **real** framing difference — rather than one of the two
cases above — is the dishonest use: it makes a genuine mismatch between your
candidate and the reference disappear from the report instead of showing up as
`content`/`rms`/`union residual`. Pin to a box
you can name a reason for, and read the unpinned framing line first when you are not
sure whether you have one.

⚠️ **The framing is over the frames you compare, and `check` decides it PER SET.**
Point it at a skeleton root and each animation directory under it is asked its own
question first: *do this set's own drawn pixels land in the box `frames.json`
records?* The sets that do are measured in that box, which is exact — it is not an
estimate of where the frames were drawn, it is where they were drawn — and nothing
another set does can move them. The sets that do not are measured in **one shared
framing** fitted across every set, printed as the header's `shared box` line, plus
their own whole-pixel MAE refinement off it (§9.2) — the fit is shared because more
frames condition it better; the constant offset it still leaves is per set, and
measured per set. Each set says which it got on its own `framed to` line.

Why the split falls there, both halves measured on an 8-shot character (147 frames):

- **Deciding the declared box per set is worth 15–25 MAE.** Over the union, one shot
  that is not in the frames' coordinates puts the pooled correction over the
  one-pixel threshold and the *whole root* falls back to a fit. Per set, the shots
  that qualify read what pinning by hand reads: `idle` **18.77** where a whole-root
  run read 41.59, with not one key different.
- **Fitting per set is worse, so `check` does not.** `fitFraming` registers extent,
  and extent is not alignment (see the ⚠️ in §9.2), so on a shot whose silhouette
  genuinely differs one shot's frames do not constrain the fit enough: `hit` reads
  **92.36** fitted on its own against 60.59 in the shared fit, and a two-frame stills
  set reads 101.94 against 42.98. More frames is a better-conditioned fit, so the
  fallback is deliberately the shared one.

`--framing shared` measures **every** set in the shared framing. It answers one question and it is a good one — *does a
single box serve every set?* — and it is the wrong number to read as one shot's
fidelity.

⚠️ The two are different measurements and their absolute numbers are not comparable.
The `scope` line at the top of the report says which one you got. `--viewport` pins
one box for the whole run whichever scope you ask for, because a pin is a claim
about your candidate's own coordinates and those do not change between shots.

⚠️ **`--frames <root>/<one-set>` is a third number for a set that cannot take the
declared box**, and it is the least constrained of the three: the fit has only that
set's frames to work from, where a root run's shared fit has every frame in the
skeleton. Measured on the same character, `hit` reads 60.50 at the root and 92.41
pointed at its own directory. A set that DOES take the declared box reads the same
either way — that box is not fitted to anything — so pointing at one directory is
exact for a shot you authored in the frames' coordinates and a rough estimate for
one you did not.

### 9.1 Why this exists

The validator has no way to know whether an animation is the right animation. It
parses the skeleton, steps every timeline, and refuses what is degenerate — a
`NaN` pose, a curve of the wrong length, a duration that disagrees with the last
key. A rig whose motion is backwards is none of those things. **`diff` cannot see
it either**: reversing every easing leaves the timeline count, the key count, the
curve kinds and the duration exactly where they were, so every measure it reports
is unmoved. The two tools together can tell you a file is valid Spine that closely
matches a reference's structure, while it plays a different shot.

So `check` compares pictures. It renders your candidate with the same rasteriser
that drew the reference frames, onto the same pixel grid, and reports what differs.

🔒 **It never opens the reference skeleton — only the frames.** That matters for
you specifically: it means **you may run `check` as often as you like** without
your run ceasing to be an honest authoring run. It is a loop, in the way `build` is
a loop. `bench` and `diff` against a rung's export are not — they read the answer,
and [the ladder's honesty rule](https://github.com/rig-c/core/blob/main/docs/LADDER.md) makes them a finish line you reach once.

📌 **That is also why the MAE figures quoted through this section stay.** Every one of
them is a candidate's own reading against rendered frames — the exam question, not the
answer key — so none of them narrows a reference-side measure, and a guide that censored
them would be teaching less for no gain in honesty. The criterion is under *The honesty
rule* in [LADDER.md](https://github.com/rig-c/core/blob/main/docs/LADDER.md); what it *does* seal is a score written
over a reference's own count, and no such figure appears here.

🚨 **If you drive the runtime yourself, a bone's local transform lives on
`bone.pose`.** A shot whose poses have to be *fitted* rather than read sends you
past `check` and into your own render loop over
`@esotericsoftware/spine-core` — that is §8's *"look for a second way to get the
same number"* applied to a whole pose, and it is a legitimate thing to build — §8.1
is how that search is set up so it converges. The
first thing it hits is not a subtlety. **spine-core 4.3 keeps a bone's local
transform on `bone.pose`, not on the bone**, so `bone.rotation = …` — or `.x`,
`.y`, `.scaleX` — is neither an error nor a rotation: it adds a property nothing
reads, and every frame renders as the setup pose. Write `bone.pose.rotation`.
Written on the bone, rung 8's poses read a flat 17.3; driven through `bone.pose`,
the same poses measure **2.76**.

🚨 **That trap has a twin one level up: the *setup* transform lives on
`bone.data.setupPose`, not on `bone.data`.** `BoneData` extends `PosedData`,
which carries the whole setup transform on a `setupPose` object, so
`bone.data.rotation` — or `.x`, `.y`, `.scaleX` — is `undefined`, and
`bone.data.rotation + delta` is `NaN`. Read and write it as
`bone.data.setupPose.rotation`. This one is worse to spot than the `bone.pose`
trap, because nothing on the path raises: `undefined` propagates to `NaN`, and
`NaN` serialises to `null`, so a fit writes `"px": null` into its own placements
file, the next build reads those as zero, `validate` is green and `check` runs.
⇒ **A `null` in your own placements dump is the signature of having read
`bone.data` directly** — nothing in this format is ever legitimately null. On
spineboy it costs the candidate MAE 13.0 → 114.6 with a green gate throughout.
Note that the two names are not
the same thing: `bone.data.setupPose` is
the setup transform, while `bone.setupPose()` on a `Bone` is the method that
resets `bone.pose` back to it.

🚨 **A region attachment's own offsets are cached.** `attachment.x`, `.y`,
`.rotation`, `.scaleX/.scaleY` are inputs to a quad spine-core computes once and
stores; what gets drawn is that stored quad — `computeWorldVertices` reads
`getOffsets(pose)`, never the fields — so writing them is, again, neither an
error nor a move. **Call `attachment.updateSequence()` after every write**, or
every frame renders the quad it was loaded with.

⇒ **An MAE that is identical across every pose, and that does not move for any
parameter you sweep — a bone's local transform, an attachment's offsets — is one
of these inert writes and not a wrong animation.** The parameter you swept was
never read; a wrong rig moves the number, a write to a field nothing reads
cannot.

🚨 **And the mirror image of all three: an objective that *improves by removing the
subject*.** The traps above are each *"the number will not move"*, and they train you
to distrust a still figure. The twin is a figure that moves, in the right direction,
for the wrong reason — and it is the more dangerous one, because progress is what it
looks like.

The shape is arithmetic, not a bug. **Any symmetric error over two silhouettes charges
a mismatch in both directions**, so it charges your ink that the reference has none
under *and* the reference's ink you leave bare. Give it a candidate that draws
**nothing** and only the second term survives: the score is the reference's own ink,
once, and it is a *finite, respectable-looking number*. A part that is present but
badly posed pays both terms and can score **worse than absence**. ⇒ A search with a
free enough range finds the cliff and walks off it, and every step of the walk reports
as an improvement. Synthetic illustration of the whole failure in three rows — one
part, one objective, nothing else changed:

| what the candidate does | part error |
| --- | --- |
| posed roughly right | 2.15 |
| posed badly — overlapping the wrong reference ink | 2.48 |
| **translated clean off the frame** | **1.00** |

The search reports **1.00 against 2.15** and calls it a 53 % gain. What it found was
the absence of a subject. ⚠️ **1.00 is not a coincidence in that table, it is the
construction**: absence pays the reference's ink exactly once, so on any objective
normalised by that ink, *"draw nothing"* sits at 1.0 by arithmetic — which is why it is
worth evaluating deliberately rather than discovering.

⇒ **Four defences, and the first is the cheap one.**

- **Bound the search to the frame.** A part cannot legitimately leave the picture on a
  shot whose frames all draw it, so a translation range wide enough to exit the
  viewport is a range that contains a false optimum. Bound each parameter by what the
  frames can *show*, not by what the format permits.
  - ⚠️ **And its converse, which is the easier half to get wrong: a bound has to
    *reach* what the frames show, not merely stop where they stop.** The two failures
    look nothing alike — a bound that is too wide loses a fit to the cliff, a bound
    that is too narrow loses one to a wall it never reports hitting. Bounding a
    vertical channel to the range the *rest* pose occupies is the classic case: a shot
    that drops its subject in from hundreds of pixels above the standing pose puts its
    own entry outside the search entirely, and the fitter returns the best pose *it was
    allowed*, which is the top of the box, silently. ⇒ **Take each channel's range from
    the brief and the frames — the extremes the shot actually visits — and then check
    afterwards how many converged values are sitting on a bound.** A knob resting
    exactly on its limit is the signature, and it costs one line to print.
- **Assert the part is drawn, every iteration.** Count your own ink for that part and
  reject any candidate whose count is zero or a small fraction of the reference's. This
  is one comparison and it makes the cliff unreachable rather than merely unattractive.
  - ⚠️ **Write it at the resolution the level is actually being evaluated at.** On a
    coarse-to-fine pyramid, a threshold expressed in full-resolution pixel counts
    refuses **every** coarse pose — and a rejection that fires on everything is
    indistinguishable from an objective with no gradient. You get `Infinity`, or a
    figure far worse than the same search reaches with the assert switched off, and
    nothing in either says *"your guard is the problem"*. ⇒ Express the count as a
    **fraction of the reference's ink at that same level**, so the test means the same
    thing at every rung of the pyramid.
- **Charge ink that leaves the window, because the cliff has a second entrance.** If
  your objective is computed inside a window around the reference's own drawn box —
  and it usually is, since that is what makes it cheap — then ink outside the window
  costs **nothing**, and the three defences above do not reach that: the part is still
  drawn, its count is still healthy, and the score still falls. The fitter hangs a part
  a few hundred pixels below the frame and reports progress every step. ⇒ **Count your
  own ink further than a small margin outside the reference's drawn box and charge it.**
  One line, in the same place as the ink count, and it closes the entrance the bound
  closes only when the bound happens to be tight enough.
- **Read the objective's floor before you trust its direction.** Evaluate *"draw
  nothing"* once, deliberately, and keep the figure. Any score at or below it is the
  cliff, whatever the search says — and if your best honest pose is *above* that floor,
  the objective is ranking absence over effort and needs an asymmetry (charge bare
  reference ink more than stray candidate ink) before it is safe to optimise against.

📌 **`check` itself is not exposed to this** — its `MAE in it` and `share` columns
divide over the **reference's** own drawn pixels and a chain that draws nothing reads
0 % on 0 slots, which §9.2 says is the loudest row in the table and not the quietest.
The trap lives in the objectives **you** write inside a fit, where the denominator is
yours to choose.

🚨 **The cliff's nearest cousin, and the one that survives all four defences:
*sacrificial cover*.** Every defence above protects a part from being **removed**. None
protects a part from being **moved somewhere wrong on purpose**. A whole-figure objective
scores one number over every pixel, so when part A is mis-placed and leaves reference ink
bare, the cheapest available improvement is frequently to drag **part B off its own correct
place to cover that ink**. Both parts are drawn, both counts are healthy, nothing leaves
the window — and the score genuinely falls, because covering bare ink is worth more to a
blunt objective than B's own displacement costs it.

⚠️ **What makes it expensive is that the objective is not lying.** The pose it prefers
really is better *by that measure*. So the loop offers no signal at all: the fit converges,
the number improves, and what you have is one part visibly out of place standing in for
another. It surfaces later as a **drift** on the sacrificed part — a slot several pixels
from where the frames put it inside a pose whose overall figure looks fine — which is the
one measure that reads parts individually.
